title: Linux Essentials
subtitle: Guess the hidden Linux terms — spin for consonants, buy vowels

puzzles.hint: The official specification that defines where directories like /bin, /etc, and /var live on a Linux system.
puzzles.explain: The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) defines the directory structure and directory contents in Linux distributions. It ensures that software and users know where to find files such as binaries in /bin, configuration in /etc, and variable data in /var.

puzzles.hint: A special permission on a shared directory that prevents users from deleting files they do not own.
puzzles.explain: When the sticky bit is set on a directory (shown as 't' in ls -l), only the file owner, the directory owner, or root can delete or rename files inside it. /tmp is the classic example because many users write there.

puzzles.hint: A named value stored in the shell that programs can read, such as PATH or HOME.
puzzles.explain: Environment variables pass configuration information to processes. For example, the PATH variable tells the shell which directories to search when you type a command name without a full path.

puzzles.hint: The tool that installs, updates, and removes software while handling all its dependencies automatically.
puzzles.explain: Package managers such as apt on Debian/Ubuntu and dnf on Fedora/RHEL download software from repositories, resolve dependency chains, and maintain a database of installed packages so the system stays consistent.

puzzles.hint: The unique number the kernel assigns to every running process so it can be tracked and managed.
puzzles.explain: Every process on a Linux system receives a unique Process Identifier (PID) at creation. Commands such as ps, top, and kill use the PID to inspect or terminate specific processes.

puzzles.hint: A task scheduled to run automatically at a specific time or interval using a crontab entry.
puzzles.explain: The cron daemon reads crontab files and executes commands at the times defined by their schedule fields (minute, hour, day, month, weekday). It is the standard Unix mechanism for automating recurring administrative tasks.

puzzles.hint: A Linux storage layer that lets you combine physical disks into flexible, resizable volumes without repartitioning.
puzzles.explain: LVM abstracts physical storage into Physical Volumes, Volume Groups, and Logical Volumes. This lets administrators resize, snapshot, and move storage dynamically without taking systems offline for repartitioning.

puzzles.hint: The encrypted protocol used to log in to remote Linux servers safely over an untrusted network.
puzzles.explain: Secure Shell (SSH) replaces older plaintext tools like Telnet by encrypting all traffic between client and server. It supports both password and public-key authentication and is the standard method for remote Linux administration.
